correctness.rationale: For every simple graph with at most seven vertices, no matching has four edges, so its matching complex has dimension <=2 and all H1 torsion equals torsion of coker(boundary_2), as im(boundary_1) is free. Independently reconstructed every one of the 1,253 networkx Graph Atlas representatives (orders 0 through 7), enumerated all disjoint pairs/triples of graph edges, built the actual signed integer second boundary and ran exact SymPy Smith normal form on every matrix. Exactly 40 graphs have SNF nonunit invariants, each a single 3; histogram edges 13:1,14:3,15:9,16:10,17:8,18:5,19:2,20:1,21:1. The unique 13-edge G1105 has f=(13,42,30), SNF (1^29,3), and the original explicit integral certificate independently satisfies boundary_2(c)=3z. This census is exhaustive conditional on published Graph Atlas completeness; modular rank alone would not certify the integer torsion. Only up-to-7 graph order is proved.
residual_risks: The independent enumeration used the standard Graph Atlas provider rather than byte-diffing packaged atlas.g6; atlas completeness is an external input.

value.rationale: Finding the first graph order at which matching-complex 3-torsion occurs, sharp sparsest edge threshold, a unique sparse witness, and the complete finite classification are natural extremal/homological boundary questions. The 40-case integer torsion table is not a repetition of known K7 torsion and offers concrete data for edge-deletion phenomena. The 7-vertex cutoff is a complete finite invariant, not an arbitrary case slice.
residual_risks: Cannot infer minimum edge count for graphs on eight or more vertices; no global matching-complex torsion theorem is claimed.

limitations: Conclusions apply to graph order <=7, not larger graphs or arbitrary flag complexes.
Smith over integers, rather than mod-3 rank alone, is the decisive exhaustive test.
